messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Kai, a 46-year-old auditor from a coastal town in the Pacific, lost his wife in a tsunami that swept through their village five years ago. He had been at work that afternoon, checking spreadsheets, when the first tremor sent his colleagues running. By the time he reached the shoreline, the water had already receded and then surged back, carrying debris and bodies. He never found her. The memory now returns not as a coherent story but as a sensory assault: he can smell the salt and rotting vegetation, taste the grit of seawater on his tongue, and yet the whole event feels so extreme that he sometimes doubts it really happened—a detail he mentions with a hollow laugh, as if his own mind is playing tricks. When he feels happy or even mildly relaxed, that fleeting sense of ease instantly dissolves: the pleasure itself becomes a trigger. In those moments he notices the particular stillness in the air—unusual silence that makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen—and the memory of that afternoon rushes back, complete with the taste of brine. Happiness, for Kai, no longer feels safe; it is a prelude to loss.

He has developed a quiet set of strategies to manage these intrusions. He avoids talking about the tsunami with anyone, because the words themselves seem to summon the smell and the helplessness. He also avoids relaxing deliberately: he keeps his evenings filled with tasks—reviewing client files, fixing small things around his apartment—because letting go of vigilance feels like inviting disaster. He smokes more now, a pack a day, though he tells himself it is just something to do with his hands. The smoking does calm him for a moment, but afterward he only feels more numb, more convinced that he cannot stop bad things from happening, and that awareness makes him scan for threats even more carefully. The world, he has come to believe, is a dangerous place, and his own helplessness is the core truth of it.

His job as an auditor has become a refuge precisely because it requires him to inspect details over and over. But he now avoids going anywhere unfamiliar; he cannot assess the danger in a new building or a street he does not know, so he takes the same route to work every day. Delays, even small ones—a train that is two minutes late, a meeting that runs over—trigger a sharp spike of threat: he assumes something bad is happening, perhaps a disaster that he cannot see. At night, waking in the dark, he lies still listening for a sound that does not come, and the silence terrifies him more than noise ever would. That fear loops back into the memory: he hears the quiet before the wave hit.

Kai’s numbness has deepened over time. He tells his therapist that he feels dead inside, and he knows his avoidance of relaxation keeps him from ever testing whether safety is possible. The less he relaxes, the more his body stays in alarm, and the more his negative appraisals—the world is dangerous, I can’t stop bad things—are confirmed. When he does briefly let his guard down, for instance while enjoying a sunny afternoon on his balcony, the happiness itself becomes a trigger: he suddenly smells the ocean, tastes salt, and the memory overwhelms him, reinforcing his belief that pleasure is a trap. That cycle has narrowed his life to a tight corridor of work, home, and controlled routes. He came to therapy only after his supervisor mentioned that his avoidance of unfamiliar client sites was affecting his performance. What frightens Kai most is not the memory itself but the possibility that he will never trust a moment of peace again—and he is beginning to wonder if that suspicion is already true.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals -> Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause the trauma memory to be recalled.
- Negative Appraisals -> Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause events to become triggers.
- Memory -> Threat: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly leads to a sense of threat.
- Memory -> Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory causes events to become triggers.
- Maladaptive Strategies -> Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause events to become triggers.

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
"The world, he has come to believe, is a dangerous place, and his own helplessness is the core truth of it."
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This conviction makes him more likely to suddenly recall the tsunami unbidden, as though the memory itself is the only proof that his helplessness is real.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
"He cannot stop bad things from happening, and that awareness makes him scan for threats even more carefully."
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he already believes he cannot stop disaster, ordinary delays like a two-minute-late train now feel like imminent warnings, turning neutral events into powerful triggers.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
"The memory now returns not as a coherent story but as a sensory assault: he can smell the salt and rotting vegetation, taste the grit of seawater on his tongue, and yet the whole event feels so extreme that he sometimes doubts it really happened—a detail he mentions with a hollow laugh, as if his own mind is playing tricks."
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When this memory intrudes, it brings with it a raw sense of immediate threat—his chest tightens, his pulse races, as if the wave is about to crash over him again.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
"The memory now returns not as a coherent story but as a sensory assault: he can smell the salt and rotting vegetation, taste the grit of seawater on his tongue, and yet the whole event feels so extreme that he sometimes doubts it really happened—a detail he mentions with a hollow laugh, as if his own mind is playing tricks."
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This memory has made him hyper-attuned to any sensory match—so that the taste of brine or the smell of salt now instantly triggers a full trauma replay, turning otherwise harmless sensations into potent triggers.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
"He also avoids relaxing deliberately: he keeps his evenings filled with tasks—reviewing client files, fixing small things around his apartment—because letting go of vigilance feels like inviting disaster."
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This constant busyness has backfired: any unexpected stillness—a few minutes of waiting for a delayed train or an unfilled gap in his schedule—now itself triggers a sharp sense of threat, as his mind interprets any pause as a sign that danger is approaching.
<<<END>>>
